title: "Bayes Scenario: Nutrition Intervention in Myanmar"
author: "Cory Whitney"
date: "2025-09-20"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

Assume data for a hypothetical nutrition intervention in Myanmar. 

Expert Prior: A nutrition program is expected to reduce child stunting by 5-15 percentage points (90% confidence interval).

Observed Data: A small pilot study in one village showed a reduction of 8 percentage points.

## 1. Simple Bayesian Update Function

### Define the Expert Prior (90% CI: 5% to 15% reduction)

```{r}
prior_lower <- 5
prior_upper <- 15
prior_mean <- (prior_lower + prior_upper) / 2  # = 10
prior_sd <- (prior_upper - prior_lower) / (2 * 1.645)  # ≈ 3.04
```

### Define the Observed Data (from a small pilot study)

```{r}
observed_mean <- 8   # 8 percentage point reduction
observed_sd <- 4     # High uncertainty because it's a small pilot

# Number of posterior samples to generate
n_samples <- 10000
```

### Perform Bayesian Update (Normal-Normal Conjugate)

The posterior mean is a weighted average of prior and observed data

```{r}

posterior_mean <- (prior_mean/prior_sd^2 + observed_mean/observed_sd^2) / 
                  (1/prior_sd^2 + 1/observed_sd^2)

posterior_sd <- sqrt(1 / (1/prior_sd^2 + 1/observed_sd^2))
```

### Generate samples from prior and posterior

```{r}
prior_samples <- rnorm(n_samples, prior_mean, prior_sd)
posterior_samples <- rnorm(n_samples, posterior_mean, posterior_sd)
```

```{r}
# Print results
cat("Expert Prior: ", prior_mean, "% reduction (90% CI: ", prior_lower, "-", prior_upper, ")\n")
cat("Observed Data: ", observed_mean, "% reduction (SD = ", observed_sd, ")\n")
cat("Posterior: ", round(posterior_mean, 1), "% reduction (90% CI: ", 
    round(quantile(posterior_samples, 0.05), 1), "-", 
    round(quantile(posterior_samples, 0.95), 1), ")\n")
```

## 2. Visualize the Results

### Plot the prior and posterior distributions

```{r}

hist(prior_samples, breaks = 50, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.5), 
     main = "Bayesian Update: Nutrition Intervention Impact",
     xlab = "Reduction in Stunting (%)", xlim = c(0, 20),
     ylab = "Density", freq = FALSE)

hist(posterior_samples, breaks = 50, col = rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.5), add = TRUE, freq = FALSE)

legend("topright", 
       legend = c("Expert Prior", "Posterior (Prior + Data)"),
       fill = c(rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.5), rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.5)))

# Add vertical lines for means
abline(v = prior_mean, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(v = posterior_mean, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```

## 3. Interpretation of Results

When you run this code, you'll see something like:

Expert Prior: 10% reduction (90% CI: 5-15)
Observed Data: 8% reduction (SD = 4)
Posterior: 8.7% reduction (90% CI: 7.2-10.2)
What this means:

The expert prior was a 10% reduction with wide uncertainty (5-15%)

The pilot study showed an 8% reduction but with high uncertainty

The posterior is a compromise: 8.7% reduction with narrower uncertainty (7.2-10.2%)

The posterior is pulled slightly toward the observed data but maintains the expert's wisdom about the plausible range. The uncertainty is reduced because we combined two sources of information.

## 4. Even Simpler Version (If You Want Minimal Code)

```{r}

# Minimal Bayesian Update
prior <- c(mean = 10, sd = 3.04)  # Expert: 10% ± 3.04
data <- c(mean = 8, sd = 4)       # Pilot: 8% ± 4
```

### Update formula

```{r}
post_mean <- (prior["mean"]/prior["sd"]^2 + data["mean"]/data["sd"]^2) / 
             (1/prior["sd"]^2 + 1/data["sd"]^2)
post_sd <- sqrt(1 / (1/prior["sd"]^2 + 1/data["sd"]^2))
```

```{r}
cat("Posterior: ", round(post_mean, 1), "% ± ", round(post_sd, 1), "%")
```

This gives you the essence of Bayesian updating: combining expert knowledge with empirical evidence in a mathematically rigorous way!
